### Session 2 durable technique findings

**(a) The stub-blocking mechanism is broader than "empty stub inlined away".**
A `return 0;` stub also lets MWCC constant-fold the *caller's* test of the
return value: a caller written `if (callee(i) == 0) { ... }` loses the call,
the test, AND its whole stack frame. Confirmed on `autoMovement19_foulBall`
(capped at 59.17% for exactly this reason, with correct source).

**(b) A hub does not need to reach 100% to deliver its unblocking value.**
Caller codegen depends only on the call site (argument setup, the `bl`, and
how the return value is consumed), not the callee's body — provided the
callee is too large to inline. So giving a large hub a real, correct,
non-trivial body restores every caller's call site even while the hub itself
sits far below 100%. This makes large dispatchers worth implementing early
even though they can't be finished in one pass.

**(c) Pointer-local SCOPE OF ASSIGNMENT is a distinct register-allocation
lever from pointer-vs-array.** Measured on `fn_3_49EA8` this session, three
steps, same semantics throughout:
- `InMemFielder* fielder = &g_Fielders[i];` initialized at top, used for every
  store: **89.86%**
- array indexing for the two tail stores, pointer for the rest: **98.92%**
- `InMemFielder* fielder;` declared uninitialized at top, array indexing for
  all stores OUTSIDE the main `if` block, and `fielder = &g_Fielders[i];`
  assigned only INSIDE that block: **100%**

The tell that a given store wants array indexing: the target re-derives the
`g_Fielders` base into a fresh register (`lis`/`addi`/`add`) for that store
instead of reusing the live base register.

**(d) `autoMovementDetermineWhatToDo` used the same shape** (array indexing
for the three trailing `presetLocationCategory` stores, pointer local for the
dense middle) and reached 100%.

### Session 2 `.bss` shape finding: `lbl_3_bss_C8`

`lbl_3_bss_C8` (.bss:0x0, 0xA4 bytes, file-local) shape, derived from its only
two reference sites (`fn_3_2E41C` and `minigameDashUpdateFieldingVariables`):
```
0x00 : 4 bytes  — NOT determined by any evidence in this unit; do not guess
0x04 : element[4], stride 0x28 (read directly off `mulli r4, idx, 0x28` at both sites)
       each element = s16[20]; entries [0..18] (offsets 0x00-0x24) are shifted
       out into fielderControlStick_continuousAngleHistory every update via an
       `lhau`-based 19-iteration backward copy; entry [19] (offset 0x26) is never
       touched by that copy
```
4 + 4*0x28 = 0xA4 exactly. `idx` is a controller-port id from a
`g_Minigame+0x18f2`/`+0x18cc` lookup, with a `-1` sentinel for "unassigned" —
consistent with 4 GameCube controller ports (`g_Controls` is indexed by the
same id at stride 0x10). Purpose: a per-controller staging buffer of recent
control-stick angle samples feeding the persistent
`fielderControlStick_continuousAngleHistory`.

Also: `currentStickDirection` and `fielderControlStick_continuousAngleHistory`
are both `lha`-accessed, i.e. `s16`.

**The leading 4 bytes of `lbl_3_bss_C8` are undetermined and must not be given
a fabricated type or name.**

### THE central constraint: stub callees are inlined away

MWCC (`-O4,p -inline deferred`) inlines an empty `return;` stub callee and
DELETES the call site entirely, so a caller can NEVER match while any of its
in-file callees is still a stub. Confirmed on `fn_3_33D9C`, `fn_3_40D54`,
`autoMovement0_stayStill_exceptForSpecialActions`.

Diagnostic escape hatch (VERIFIED WORKING, but scaffolding only — never leave it
in the source): bracket the *stub callee* in
`#pragma dont_inline on` / `#pragma dont_inline reset`. This preserves the call
and lets you validate the caller's source shape immediately. Measured:
`autoMovement0_stayStill_exceptForSpecialActions` 23.25% -> **100%** with the
pragma, back to 23.25% once reverted.

Consequence: `autoMovement0_stayStill_exceptForSpecialActions`'s C source in the
tree is **CONFIRMED CORRECT** and will reach 100% automatically the moment
`updateFielderPositionAndVelocityForSpecialActions` gets a real body. Do not
re-grind it. Same likely holds for `fn_3_33D9C` / `fn_3_40D54`, whose bodies are
written and whose only blocker is `autoMovementDetermineWhatToDo`.

Call-graph survey (which functions are blocked and on what) is at
`build/.match_grind/fielder_callgraph.md`. Highest-leverage stub callees
to implement next, by number of in-file callers: `setFielderVelocity` (13),

### Fielder base address: pointer local vs. array indexing

`InMemFielder* fielder = &g_Fielders[fielderIndex];` is the right source shape
whenever the target materialises the base into a register (`add rN, r0, rM`) and
then uses plain displacement accesses off it. Plain `g_Fielders[i].field`
indexing only reproduces the target in the simplest cases (one global live, no
offset-0 member access). Measured both ways:
- `fn_3_530EC` 79.71% -> **100%** purely from switching to the pointer local
  (array indexing emitted an indexed `lfsx` for the offset-0 `pos.x` read).
- `fn_3_27738` 98.18% -> **100%** from the same switch (array indexing put the
  `mulli` result in the wrong register once `g_Ball` was also live).
- `fn_3_3A1FC` matched at 100% with plain array indexing — only `g_Fielders` was
  live and no offset-0 member was touched.

### Float literals: use the named target rodata label

Target float constants show as `lbl_3_rodata_XXXX` relocations. Writing `0.0f`
pools an anonymous `@NNN` and objdiff scores it as a CONST_POOL mismatch.
`extern const f32 lbl_3_rodata_B20;` (declaration, per the precedent in
`src/menus/rep_1028.c`) fixes it — `fn_3_3A1FC` 99.29% -> 100%.
The *definition* form (`const f32 lbl_3_rodata_B20 = 0.0f;`) was tested and is
WRONG: it emits an extra local `.rodata` symbol at offset 0x60 instead of the
target's offset 0, leaving `.text` worse and inflating `.rodata`% spuriously.
`lbl_3_rodata_B20` is the float `0.0f`.

      locals need to be `int`, not `s16`, and both need to be named locals
      (not inlined call expressions), to reproduce the target exactly.

Lesson: implement large hubs EARLY; do not wait until they are finishable. A
hub delivers its full unblocking value at partial completion, because the
caller's codegen only depends on the call site, and a hub that big can never
be inlined into anyone.

### Other durable technique findings (session 3)

(e) **`int` vs `s16` for an angle local is an `extsh`-placement lever**, needed
    in BOTH directions: `fn_3_2B5C0` needed `int` locals to FORCE the target's
    `extsh` placement; `fn_3_3AAF8` needed `int` to SUPPRESS one. Check the
    declared width of every angle/short local against the target's `extsh`
    positions before grinding anything else.
(f) **A trailing early-return guard can get fused into a single `bnelr`** by
    MWCC when the target keeps it unfused. Symptom is a control-flow AND
    function-size mismatch at the tail. Fix: combine it with the preceding
    guard into one `||` condition. This closed the size mismatch on
    `fn_3_3ABF0`.
(g) **MWCC's own loop unrolling can reproduce a hand-unrolled target.**
    `processFielderAutoCatch` matched 100% first try as a plain 9-iteration
    `for` over `g_Fielders`. Do not hand-unroll to chase an unrolled target.

Generalizable finding (promote-candidate for `docs/matching_notes.md`):
for a `u8`/`s8` struct member assigned a small negative constant, MWCC's
immediate-encoding choice for the store value (`li r0,-1` sign-form vs
`li r0,0xff` zero-extended form) is driven by the field's declared
signedness in the struct, not by the literal token written at the call
site. `-1`, `0xFF`, and `(u8)-1`/`(s8)-1` casts on the RHS all compiled
identically once the destination is a fixed `u8` field -- the implicit
truncating conversion to the field's own declared type erases any
information carried by the literal's form. Only changing the field's
declared type from `u8` to `s8` changed the emitted immediate. This
generalizes the existing `int` vs `s16` "declared width, not register
contents" lever from `fn_3_2B5C0`/`fn_3_3AAF8` to declared signedness for
narrow direct stores, not just comparisons.

## Session 5

### Derived real signature

`int adjustPlayerPosOutsideFoulLine(int fielderIndex, VecXYZ* out)`.

Evidence from the target asm:
- `mulli r6, r3, 0x268` on entry, immediately followed by `lis/addi
  g_Fielders` + `add` — the standard fielder-index-into-`g_Fielders[9]`
  base pattern used throughout this file, confirming `r3` is
  `int fielderIndex`.
- The tail (`stfs f3, 0x0(r4)` / `stfs f2, 0x8(r4)`) writes two floats at
  offsets 0x0 and 0x8 of `r4` — that is `VecXYZ.x` (offset 0) and
  `VecXYZ.z` (offset 8), skipping `y` (offset 4) — a `VecXYZ*` output
  parameter, matching convention #7 (component-wise field writes rather
  than whole-struct assignment).
- Cross-checked against the sole caller in `game/rep_AC8.s` /
  `fielder.s` (`bl adjustPlayerPosOutsideFoulLine` inside
  `updateFielderPosition_checkFielderCollision`): `r3`/`r4` are not
  reloaded immediately before the call — they still hold the caller's own
  `fielderIndex` and pointer-out parameters (saved into `r29`/`r30` right
  after the caller's prologue but never overwritten before the `bl`),
  confirming the same `(int, VecXYZ*)` parameter pair is threaded straight
  through.
- Return value: after the call, the caller only does `cmplwi r3, 0x0` and
  branches on that, so the function does return an `int`, but the
  fall-through path to the two `stfs` at the end does **not** set `r3` to
  any specific value before `blr` — it just returns 1 (`li r3,1; blr`)
  from the early-exit branch, and otherwise falls off the end leaving
  whatever incidental value is left in `r3` from earlier computations
  (a `1.0f`-comparison spill of `int 2` in one build, arbitrary in ours).
  This is the same "no explicit return statement on the fall-through path"
  pattern noted as an accepted idiom elsewhere in this codebase; the C
  source has no `return` at the end of the function body.

Header (`include/game/fielding/fielder.h`) updated to the new
signature. `#include "game/UnknownHomes_Game.h"` added to the header
(previously only `mssbTypes.h`) because `VecXYZ` is defined there and the

### Plain-English body logic

Given the fielder's *next-frame* position (`pos + velocity` for x and z):

1. Push the point away from the origin along whichever of x/z is smaller
   in magnitude, halfway toward matching the larger one (a soft diagonal
   foul-line clamp: `x`/`z` get nudged toward `|x| == |z|`, keeping the
   larger magnitude untouched and updating the other to be an average of
   itself and the boundary).
2. Then check the result against a "cone" around `base_MoundCoordinates[2]`
   (offset `z` from the mound within `±x`); if inside that cone, apply the
   same halfway nudge again, this time relative to the mound's `z`
   coordinate rather than the origin.
3. Finally, if the resulting `z` is at or below `base_MoundCoordinates[2].x`
   (note: `.x` of the *coordinate*, not a typo for `z` again — that's what
   the target asm loads), return `1` without writing to `*out` (caller
   treats a `1` return as "already fine, skip"). Otherwise write the
   adjusted `x`/`z` into `*out`.

### Remaining gap at instruction level (74.71%, NOT exhausted)

Our function is 284 bytes; target is 332 bytes (48 bytes / 12 instructions
short). All of the remaining diff is one recurring, unexplained pattern:
at every one of the 4 sites where the code loads the `0.5` constant
(`lbl_3_rodata_B80`) for the halfway-nudge multiply, the target computes
the constant's address in two steps and reuses a register for scratch
across an unrelated dead value:
```
lis  r3, lbl_3_rodata_B80@ha
addi r5, r3, lbl_3_rodata_B80@l
li   r3, 0x2          <- dead, unused by the following lfs
lfs  f1, 0x0(r5)
```
whereas ours (correctly, using the same named symbol) collapses this to
the equivalent 2-instruction form:
```
lis r5, lbl_3_rodata_B80@ha
lfs f1, lbl_3_rodata_B80@l(r5)
```
The target also reloads `lbl_3_rodata_B20` (0.0f) a second time via a
fresh `lis r3, ...@ha; lfs f0, ...@l(r3)` for its second use partway
through the function instead of keeping it live in a register, and
recomputes `-x` (`fneg f5, f3`) as a fresh instruction at a point where

### THE session-7 finding worth carrying to other files

**A dead-looking `li rN, <small const>` in the target is usually a status
local you have not modelled.** `adjustPlayerPosOutsideFoulLine` sat at 74.71%
for a whole session with a 12-instruction gap that session 5 wrote off as an
inexplicable scheduling artifact: at four sites the target computed a float
constant's address in the split `lis`/`addi` form and then emitted an
apparently-dead `li r3, 0x2`. The real explanation is that r3 held an int
return-status local (`li r3,0` at entry, `li r3,2` at each of four branches,
`li r3,1` on the early exit, returned on the write path). Needing r3 free for
that value is precisely what forced the split address form at every constant
load. Adding the local took it to 92.95% in one step.

Generalisation: when a function's C source discards a return value the target
computes, the cost is NOT confined to the return instruction — it distorts
register allocation across the whole function and shows up as "unexplained
scheduling noise" far from the actual return. Before writing off a
register-allocation gap in an int-returning function, list every `li r3, <const>`
in the target that is NOT immediately followed by `blr`, and check that your C
models each one.

Corollary confirmed the same session: this lever is spent once applied. An asm
scan of the file's other int-returning near-misses
(`updateFielderPosition_checkFielderCollision`, `fn_3_4DB84`) found both
already model their r3 status values correctly, and neither moved.

- `adjustPlayerPosOutsideFoulLine`: declaring `x` before `z`, and moving

  f3/f2, ours in f1/f5) plus one extra constant reload; no statement

- `fielding_setStartingCoordinates`: the target's `neg;orc;srawi;+2` idiom for

### CORRECTION to session 7: `updateOutfielderPositionBasedOnBallState` is NOT "register colouring only"
Session 7 recorded all three near-misses as differing from target purely in register
colour. That is wrong for this one. Its 8 remaining mismatches (139/139 instructions,
556/556 bytes) split into two unrelated causes:

```
[8]  ARG  target: lbz r8, 0x11(r3)                 ours: lbz r7, 0x11(r3)
[9]  ARG  target: lha r7, 0xb0(r4)                 ours: lha r8, 0xb0(r4)
[10] ARG  target: cmplwi r8, 0x0                   ours: cmplwi r7, 0x0
[11] ARG  target: mr r6, r7                        ours: mr r6, r8
[38] ARG  target: cmpwi r7, 0x6                    ours: cmpwi r8, 0x6
[40] ARG  target: cmplwi r8, 0x0                   ours: cmplwi r7, 0x0
[43] ARG  target: lis r5, lbl_3_rodata_B20@ha      ours: lis r5, @1269@ha
[46] ARG  target: lfs f0, lbl_3_rodata_B20@l(r5)   ours: lfs f0, @1269@l(r5)
```
- Six are an r7/r8 colour swap between the `g_d_GameSettings.minigamesEnabled` byte and
  `g_FieldingLogic.selectedFielder`.
- **Two are a CONST_POOL mismatch and are structurally unfixable while this file is
  incomplete.** `@1269` is the anonymous pooled `0.0f` emitted by the `x > 0.0f` test
  inside `dolsqrtf2`, which is an `inline` function in the SHARED header
  `include/stl/math.h` (line ~153). We cannot make that literal reference
  `lbl_3_rodata_B20` without editing a shared header used by other units.

  Root cause, and it matters for the whole file: **`lbl_3_rodata_B20` IS this TU's
  pooled `0.0f`.** In the original build every `0.0f` literal in the TU pooled into one
  `.rodata` entry that dtk labelled `lbl_3_rodata_B20`. Our workaround declares it
  `extern const f32`, which makes it an undefined external — so any genuine `0.0f`
  literal we cannot rewrite (i.e. one inside a shared inline) pools separately as
  `@NNN`. This resolves itself only when enough of the file is written that the real
  pool can be defined in the target's order and the `extern` workaround dropped.
  Do NOT hack `include/stl/math.h` to work around it; the same `@NNN` symptom is
  already logged for `setIntendedLocToInterceptBall` (session 4, item (c)).

Consequence: `updateOutfielderPositionBasedOnBallState` **cannot reach 100% until the
file's `.rodata` pool is real**, regardless of how the r7/r8 swap is resolved.

### THE session-8 finding worth carrying to other files

**This file's residual register-colouring gaps are immune to every source-level and
configuration-level lever available.** Across sessions 5, 7 and 8, three functions whose
diffs are (or are almost entirely) pure register permutation have now resisted roughly
fifteen structurally distinct hypotheses spanning:
- statement and declaration reordering, in both directions;
- pointer-local vs. array-indexing for the base address;
- combined vs. split vs. compound-assignment vs. interleaved initializers;
- introducing or removing named temporaries for constants and intermediates;
- expression regrouping and guard/branch restructuring;
- every adjacent compiler version and every plausible codegen flag.

In several cases the variants compiled to **byte-identical code**, which is the useful
signal: MWCC had already normalized the difference, so the source shape was never the
variable. When a diff is a *pure* register permutation with identical opcodes, offsets,
count and control flow, treat that as evidence that the cause is TU-wide context
(constant-pool state, and what else in the translation unit is competing for registers)
rather than the function's own source shape — and stop grinding it.

Corollary, specific to this file: the near-misses are gated on the FILE being finished,
not on cleverer source for the individual function. `updateOutfielderPositionBasedOnBallState`
is the proof — two of its eight mismatches are literally caused by the incomplete-file
`extern lbl_3_rodata_B20` workaround. Expect some of this class to resolve for free as
the remaining stub functions get real bodies. **Grinding them further before then is
negative-expected-value.**

### Session 9 round 2 — FMA fusion lever, missed-inline negative, and a canary false alarm

`.text` PER-UNIT 5.5645523% -> **6.0460286%**. `.rodata`/`.data`/`.bss` unchanged
(37.037037% / 80.55556% / 46.451614%). Functions at 100%: still 22.

#### NEW LEVER (the most valuable finding of this session): FMA fusion is source-controllable

MWCC fuses `a*a + b*b` into `fmuls` + `fmadds`. The target sometimes does this and
sometimes emits the fully unfused `fmuls` + `fmuls` + `fadds`. Which one you get is
controlled by whether the squares are written into explicit named `f32` temporaries:

- `dist = dolsqrtf2(dx * dx + dz * dz);`            -> MWCC FUSES (`fmadds`)
- `dx2 = dx * dx; dz2 = dz * dz;`
  `dist = dolsqrtf2(dx2 + dz2);`                    -> MWCC does NOT fuse

This is the same underlying lever session 5 found on `adjustPlayerPosOutsideFoulLine`
(hypothesis [3], its single largest jump, 66.58% -> 74.34%) but stated generally.

CRITICAL: the correct form differs PER CALL SITE, even within one function.
`fn_3_30A58` has two `dolsqrtf2` calls — the target leaves the FIRST unfused and
partially fuses the SECOND. Splitting only the first gained 2.1 points; the second was
already correct and must be left inline. Check every sum-of-squares site individually
against the target asm; do not apply this blanket.

Measured results of applying it:
- `fn_3_30A58` first call site only: 91.31156% -> **93.39196%** (KEPT)
- `findClosestFieldersToLooseBallAndAssignToGoGetIt`: 88.13937% -> **88.93031%** (KEPT)
- `fielderAIAssignmentRelated`: 91.196075% -> 90.24313% (REGRESSION, reverted — its
  target genuinely fuses, so the inline form is correct there)

#### MEASURED NEGATIVE: do not factor the auto-movement setter idiom into a helper

`fielderAIAssignmentRelated`'s target FOLDS its two textually identical "assign
auto-movement 18" blocks into one shared block reached from both sites (it recomputes
`&g_Fielders[idx]` from the index rather than reusing a live pointer, and carries a
`cmpwi idx,-1`/`beq` guard). That is a textbook missed-inline signature, so a
`static void setFielderAutoMovement18(int fielderIndex)` helper taking the INDEX (with
the `-1` guard inside) was written and both call sites replaced.

Result: 91.196075% -> 90.117645% (REGRESSION, reverted). No compiler warning.
MWCC re-inlined the helper at both sites rather than sharing it, and the extra
structure cost a point. **Write each occurrence of the auto-movement setter idiom
inline; do not factor it out.** The target's fold is a late cross-jump/tail-merge
optimizer pass, not something reachable from source shape.

### THE session-10 finding worth carrying to other files: `const` on an extern is an alias-analysis lever

`fielding_setStartingCoordinates` sat at 90.60% for four sessions with a residual that session 4
described as "five recurring instances of a load-x/store-x/load-z/store-z target ordering that our
codegen turns into load-x/load-z/store-x/store-z (scheduler hoists the second load)". The cause was
not statement shape — it was that the five coordinate tables were declared `extern const VecXZ ...`.
`const` tells MWCC a store through an unrelated `f32*` out-param cannot alias the table, which
licenses hoisting the second load above the first store. Dropping `const` from the six extern
declarations restored the target's strict load/store interleaving: **90.59731% -> 99.05369% in one
change.**

This is also a correctness fix, not a matching hack, and there is a cheap general test for it:
**a symbol that lives in `.data` rather than `.rodata` was not `const` in the original source.**
All five tables are `.data` symbols. Check the section of every `extern const` you write against
`config/*/symbols.txt`; if it is not in `.rodata`, the `const` is wrong and is silently costing you
load/store scheduling. A census of this file's other 21 `const` externs found all of them correctly
in `.rodata`, so the sweep is now complete here.

### Second finding: a target that materialises a loop constant into a register is telling you it was a loop

`fn_3_42BD0` sat at 88.45% and was marked "hypotheses exhausted" in session 4, whose diagnosis was
that target's `li r0,N; cmpw r0,r3` versus our compact `cmpwi r3,N` was "an MWCC
scheduling quirk unrelated to source-level comparison direction". It was not a quirk. Materialising
the comparison constant into a register, plus a fielder pointer stepped by `addi r4,r4,0x268`
rather than folded into a displacement, is the signature of a **fully unrolled loop**: after
unrolling, the loop counter is still a variable, so each copy re-materialises its now-constant value
instead of folding it into the compare. Rewriting three hand-written per-outfielder blocks as a
plain `for (n = 6; n < 9; n++)` took it 88.44776% -> 98.43284% immediately, and then to **100%** by
dropping the loop-carried pointer and indexing `g_Fielders[n]` directly in the body.

Generalisation: `li rN, <const>` immediately before a `cmpw` against a loop-invariant, in code that
looks like repeated parallel blocks, means the original was a loop. This is the mirror image of the
already-logged session-3 finding (g) that MWCC's unroller reproduces a hand-unrolled target — the
same fact read from the other direction, and far more actionable.

### Third finding: `dolsqrtf2`'s pooled constants are a PER-FUNCTION lever, not a file-wide one

The anonymous `@NNNN` constant-pool symptom logged since session 4 was fully identified this
session. `include/stl/math.h`'s `dolsqrtf2` is `static inline` and its four float literals pool as
compiler-generated anonymous entries where the target names them:
`@1420`=`lbl_3_rodata_B20` (0.0f), `@1421`=`B30` (0.5 double), `@1422`=`B38` (3.0 double),
`@1423`=`B40` (0.0 double). 102 instruction rows across 8 functions referenced them.

A TU-local clone of `dolsqrtf2` that references those four as named externs (added as
`static inline f32 fielderSqrt(f32 x)` in this file — `include/stl/math.h` was NOT touched) drops
the pool-row count from 102 to 6. But applying it at every call site in the file was measured and is
NET NEGATIVE: it improved two functions and regressed six, and collapsed `.rodata` from 37.037% to
24.026% because nothing was left to emit the two doubles.

Applied at only the call sites inside `fn_3_30A58` and `fielding_prePitchAutomovement` it gained
+3.12 and +1.82 points with zero regressions and `.rodata` unchanged. Both are functions where the
split symbol had forced `0.0f` into TWO registers at once, costing an extra callee-save `f27` and a
larger stack frame — that is the tell for where this lever pays. Use it per call site, never
file-wide; the same per-site discipline session 9 established for FMA fusion.

### A REAL BUG was found and fixed, not just a matching change

The `farFromLocation` test read `fielder->joggingSpeed` (offset 0x58). The target reads
**offset 0x50, `currentVelocity`**. Our source was semantically wrong, not merely
differently-scheduled. Lesson, and it is cheap to apply everywhere: when a near-miss shows
a lone `DIFF_ARG_MISMATCH` on a *displacement* (`lfs f1, 0x50(rN)` vs `lfs f1, 0x58(rN)`)
rather than on a register number, that is a WRONG FIELD in the source, not register
colouring. Read the displacement against the struct layout before assuming it is noise.

### THE session-11 finding worth carrying to other files: binding an inline helper's constants to named locals controls its FPR allocation

This is the most reusable result of the session and it moved two functions at once.

The TU-local `fielderSqrt` clone (session 10's workaround for the `@NNNN` pool symptom)
read its two Newton-iteration constants directly as file-scope externs:
```c
guess = lbl_3_rodata_B30 * guess * (lbl_3_rodata_B38 - guess * guess * xd);
```
Every inlined copy allocated {constants -> f4,f3; argument -> f2}, whereas the target
allocates {argument -> f4; 0.5 -> f3; 3.0 -> f2}. Session 10 logged this as an
unexplained "f4-vs-f2 in the inlined sqrt" residual.

Cause: the ORIGINAL `dolsqrtf2` in `include/stl/math.h` holds those two values as
**function-scope `static const double`s declared after the parameter**, not as file-scope
externs. Reading a file-scope extern makes MWCC allocate the constant's register ahead of
the argument's; a local binding does not.

Fix — bind them to named `f64` locals declared BEFORE the value locals:
```c
static inline f32 fielderSqrt(f32 x) {
    if (x > lbl_3_rodata_B20) {
        f64 half = lbl_3_rodata_B30;
        f64 three = lbl_3_rodata_B38;
        f64 xd = (f64)x;
        f64 guess = __frsqrte(xd);
        guess = half * guess * (three - guess * guess * xd);
        ...
```
Both inlined sqrt bodies then match the target EXACTLY, at every call site, in both
functions that use the helper. Declaration order within the pair matters and had to be
measured: `half` then `three` (+1.15 combined over `three` then `half`).

Generalisation for other files: **if an inlined helper's body is register-shifted by a
constant offset relative to the target, check whether its constants are file-scope externs
where the original had function-scope statics or literals.** Binding them to named locals
inside the helper, declared ahead of the value locals, is a real and cheap lever — and
unlike most register-colouring levers in this file, it worked at every call site
simultaneously.

### Second finding: stack-slot order follows REVERSE declaration order

`fielding_setStartingCoordinates(i, &outX, &outZ)` passed `&outX` as 0x14(r1) and `&outZ`
as 0x10(r1); the target has them the other way round. Simply swapping the two
declarations (`f32 outZ; f32 outX;`) fixed both rows. This works for stack-resident
locals. It does NOT work for register-resident ones — the same swap applied to the `dx`/`dz`
pair (which live in callee-saved f28/f29) changed nothing.

### Third finding: MWCC normalises loop-variable IDENTITY, not just its shape

The target uses a different register for each of the two loops' counters (r29 in loop A,
r27 in loop B); ours uses r27 for both. Giving each loop its own declared `int` variable —
tried in BOTH assignments, `int i; int n;` with either loop taking `n` — compiled
**byte-identically** to the shared-variable form in both cases. Add loop-variable identity
to the list of things MWCC normalises away (alongside statement-splitting, compound
assignment, and pointer-stepping shape, all previously logged in this file). Do not spend
another session on it.

### Tooling

### THE session-12 finding worth carrying to other files: the declared-width lever extends to bytes, and it is worth far more than register grinding

Session 3's finding (e) established that `int` vs `s16` is an `extsh`-PLACEMENT lever.
The same rule governs BYTE-width locals, with two distinct and separately-diagnosable
tells, and on `fn_3_2F7D4` fixing both took the function **70.559525% -> 92.32143% in a
single edit**, and simultaneously closed an 8-byte size excess (344 B -> exactly 336 B).

1. **`clrlslwi rD, rS, 24, N` in ours where the target has `slwi rD, rS, N`** means our
   local is declared `u8` where the original was `int`. The mask is MWCC re-narrowing a
   value it must treat as 8-bit before scaling it. Declaring the local `int` removes it.
2. **An extra `extsb` at a value's USE SITES (rather than at its load)** means our local
   is declared `s8` where the original was `int`. The target loads the parameter into a
   register once and never re-extends it; ours re-extends at every use, and also burns a
   separate register for the narrowed copy.

Generalisation, now confirmed across `s16` and `s8`/`u8`: MWCC inserts width-conversion
instructions based on the local's DECLARED width, never on what the register happens to
hold. Before grinding any register-allocation gap, read every `extsb`/`extsh`/`clrlslwi`/
`rlwinm` mask instruction that differs, and check the corresponding local's declared type.
This is far cheaper and far higher-yield than statement reordering.

### Second finding: carry signedness on the POINTER, not on the value

`(s8)*((u8*)p)` and `*((s8*)p)` are semantically identical but compile differently:
- `(s8)*((u8*)p)`  -> `lbz r0, d(rB)` ; `extsb rD, r0`   (two registers, scratch + dest)
- `*((s8*)p)`      -> `lbz rD, d(rB)` ; `extsb rD, rD`   (in place, matches target)

The value-cast form forces a scratch register and shifts colouring downstream. When the
target sign-extends a loaded byte IN PLACE, put the signedness in the pointer type.
Worth +0.24 and removed 4 mismatch rows on `fn_3_2F7D4`.

### Third finding: `x + x` versus `x * 2` is a real association lever

`apexDiv * 2 + frames3 + 2` let MWCC reassociate to `slwi; addi 2; add frames3` AND
dragged an unrelated `sth` store across the sequence with it. `apexDiv + apexDiv +
frames3 + 2` reproduces the target's `add; add; addi` order exactly. Worth +2.08.
When a target computes a doubling as `add rX,rX,rX` rather than `slwi rX,rX,1`, write the
source as `x + x`. This is NOT one of the forms MWCC normalises away.

### Fourth finding: multi-exit tail sharing is COUNTABLE, so stop guessing at it

Every textual `return <const>;` statement costs its own exit block (here `li r3,0; blr`,
8 bytes) unless several conditions are `||`-chained into ONE `return` statement, in which
case they all branch to a single shared block. That makes the grouping question
arithmetic instead of guesswork: **(our size - target size) / 8 is exactly how many extra
exit blocks you have.** Measured on `fn_3_3CB8C`, three structurally distinct groupings:

| grouping | exit blocks | size | match |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 separate `return 0;` | 6 | 316 B | 91.30137% |
| all 4 conditions in the first branch `||`-merged | 2 | 284 B | 96.9863% |
| `zone<1 || idx<6` merged, two angle tests separate | 4 | 300 B | 97.054794% |

The target has **3** exit blocks. Use the byte delta to binary-search the grouping rather
than trying shapes blind.

### Fifth finding (negative, useful): "LEAF" in the v2 call graph means NO IN-FILE CALLS

Two functions the queue lists as LEAF do make external calls: `initializeMiniGameCharacters`
calls `setFielderValues` (roster_init.c) and `fn_3_2F7D4` calls `fieldingRelatedAnimations`
(`.text:0x001682AC`, another unit). This is not an error in the classification — external
callees can never be inlined away, so they do not block — but it does mean "LEAF" does not
imply "no prototypes needed from elsewhere". Budget for that when picking queue items.

```c
void uncalledattemptJumpingCatch(int fielderIndex) {
    InMemFielder* fielder = &g_Fielders[fielderIndex];

    if (fielder->distanceFromBall > modWeightBasedFactors[fielder->ModifiedWeightForMag][2]) {
        return;
    }
    if (g_Ball.AtBat_Contact_BallPos.y < fielder->jumpY) {
        return;
    }
    if (g_Ball.AtBat_Contact_BallPos.y > fielder->jumpY + fielder->distToWhereFlyBallWillBeAtHalfFielderHeight) {
        return;
    }
    if (isCoordinateUncatchableTerrain(g_Ball.AtBat_Contact_BallPos.x, g_Ball.AtBat_Contact_BallPos.z)) {
        return;
    }

    fielder->catchAnimationFramesCountDown = 1;
    fielder->catchAnimationFramesCountUp = 0;
    fielder->catchAnimation = 6;
    fielder->catchVerticalZone = 0;
    fielder->catchCentreRightLeftOfBody = 0;
    fielder->catchFastBattedBallInd = 0;
    fielder->autoCatch0_noCatchAnimationOnly1 = 0;
    fielder->action = 0;
    fielder->wallJumpFramesTillTopOfWallContact = 0;
    fielder->wallActionFrameCounter = 0;
    fielder->wallJumpStatus = 0;
    fielder->wallActionCountDown = 0;
    fielder->caughtBallInAir = 0;
    fielder->runningCatchInd = 0;
    if (g_Ball.framesUntilBallHitsGround > 1) {

}
```

```c
void initializeMiniGameCharacters(void) {
    int i;
    g_GameLogic.rosterLoc_skippingCap = 0;
    if (g_d_GameSettings.minigamesEnabled) {
        for (i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
            s8 charId = <signed byte at g_Minigame + 0x18F4 + i>;
            if (charId >= 0) {
                int fielderIndex = (charId == (s8)g_Minigame.minigamePlayerSelectedOrder) ? 0 : (i + 2);
                InMemFielder* fielder;
                u8 handedness;
                setFielderValues(charId, fielderIndex);
                fielder = &g_Fielders[fielderIndex];
                handedness = g_Minigame.minigameControlStruct[0].battingHandedness[i];
                if (fielderIndex == 0) {

                } else {
                    fielder->lockoutDuration = fielderLockout[handedness][7];
                }

```
THREE prerequisites, in ascending order of risk:
- `extern u8 fielderLockout[2][9];` — needed, not currently declared. Symbol is
  `.data:0x000046F8 size:0x14`, and `.ghidra_cache/in_game.data.txt` independently gives
  `byte[2][9] fielderLockout`. The asm's `mulli r0, r0, 0x9` row stride and its use of
  columns 0 and 7 corroborate the `[2][9]` shape. `.data`, so NOT `const`. LOW risk.
- `setFielderValues` is declared `void setFielderValues(void)` in

  before and after to confirm it is codegen-neutral (its body is still an empty stub, so it
  should be, but verify rather than assume). MEDIUM risk.
- The `charId` array. The loop reads four consecutive SIGNED bytes at
  `g_Minigame + 0x18F4 .. 0x18F7`. Under the current header, `minigameControlStruct[2]` sits
  at 0x18CC with stride 0x16, so 0x18F4 falls inside instance [1] at struct offset 0x12 —
  i.e. `aIStrength[2]` — and reading four bytes OVERRUNS the declared `u8 aIStrength[4]`

  boundaries in 0x18E2..0x18F8 are probably wrong** — plausibly a real contiguous `s8[4]`

  fit. Either establish the real layout from independent evidence first, or use an explicit
  raw-offset expression and say so. HIGH risk — this is the reason the function was

`uncalledattemptJumpingCatch` was declared `void` (inherited from the placeholder
`void f(void)` stub pass). Its first draft compiled to 256 B against a 292 B target and
86.904106%, and the mismatch rows showed the target emitting `li r3, 0x0` immediately before
branching to the shared epilogue on each of four guard failures, plus `li r3, 0x1` on the
success path — nine instructions we did not emit at all, and 9 * 4 = 36 = exactly
292 - 256. Changing the signature to `int`, the four guards to `return 0;` and adding a
final `return 1;` took it to **100%** in one edit (together with the field fix below).

Generalisation: when our function is short by a multiple of 4 and the missing rows are
`li r3,<const>` next to branches, the declared return type is wrong. The byte arithmetic
confirms the diagnosis before you compile. This is the return-type analogue of session 12's
declared-WIDTH lever, and it is just as cheap. Every placeholder `void f(void)` stub in this
codebase is suspect on BOTH axes — parameters and return type.

### Fourth finding (negative, precisely located): fused `bXXlr` returns happen for TOP-LEVEL guards, not for guards nested inside blocks

`fn_3_555AC` sits at 70.51685%, 396 B vs 356 B — exactly 40 bytes = 5 extra exit blocks.
The target has NO stack frame and every early return is a FUSED conditional return
(`fcmpo` then a single `bgtlr`/`bltlr`/`blelr`/`bgelr`, costing zero exit-block bytes).
Ours has no stack frame either — that hypothesis was tested and REFUTED, so frame-vs-no-frame
is not the cause. Rows 0-19 are byte-identical, including the first four guards, which fuse
correctly on BOTH sides. The divergence begins at row 29: the five guards that live INSIDE
the two nested quadrant blocks emit `fcmpo` + `cror eq,gt,eq` + `bne <block>` plus a separate
exit block, instead of fusing.

So the fusion condition appears to be lexical position, not stack frame: a top-level
`if (cond) return;` fuses; the same guard nested two levels deep inside `if`/`else` blocks
does not. Untried and recommended: restructure the two quadrant blocks so those guards become
top-level `if (...) return;` statements (e.g. select the quadrant's `lo`/`hi` values first,
then run flat guards), or invert the sub-branch polarity so the returns become fallthroughs.

### THE session-14 finding worth carrying to other files: a fused conditional return comes from a POSITIVE guard, not a negated early return

This CORRECTS session 13's fourth finding, which blamed lexical nesting. Nesting is irrelevant.

`fn_3_555AC` was 396 B against a 356 B target -- exactly 40 bytes / 5 extra exit blocks. Target emitted single fused `blelr`/`bgelr` conditional returns; ours emitted `fcmpo` + `cror eq,lt,eq` (or `cror eq,gt,eq`) + `beqlr`, plus separate exit blocks.

The `cror` is the tell. On PowerPC, `ble` branches when the GT bit is FALSE (so it also takes the branch when unordered); `cror eq,lt,eq` + `beq` synthesises the strict LT|EQ predicate. MWCC emits the strict `cror` form when the source says `if (a <= b) return;` (branch-on-true of a `<=`), and the cheap loose `ble`/`bge` form when the source says `if (a > b) { ...action... }` and the guard is the fall-out. Only the second form is eligible for the peephole that fuses a branch-to-a-lone-`blr` into `bXXlr`.

Fix: rewrite each negated early-return guard as its positive complement, `&&`-chained around the action:
```c
if (posZ > -posX + lo && posZ < -posX + hi) { fielder->inBasePath = 2; }
```
instead of
```c
if (posZ <= -posX + lo) return;
if (posZ >= -posX + hi) return;
fielder->inBasePath = 2;
return;
```
One edit: 70.51685% -> 98.03371%, 396 B -> exactly 356 B, and every opcode and branch-structure difference disappeared (the 31 remaining rows are pure FPR numbering). Whenever the target has `bXXlr` where you have `cror` + a separate exit block, the source polarity is inverted -- do not go looking for stack-frame or nesting explanations.

### Second finding: which if/else arm the target lays out FIRST is a source-level lever

`fn_3_2D308` sat at 95.43011% with 4 excess bytes and 6 rows, described as a block-ordering swap. Inverting the polarity -- `if (dist >= K) { call } else { store }` becoming `if (dist < K) { store } else { call }`, logically identical -- took it to 100% with zero mismatch rows and exact size, in one edit. Same lever as the finding above, applied to a two-armed if/else rather than a guard. When the diff shows the two arms emitted in the opposite order, invert the condition rather than reordering statements.

### Third finding: `srawi` where the target has `srwi` means the shift is signed, even for a `u8` field

`fRunningTimeToDestinationPlus7` read `fielder->maxAccLength_ConstF >> 1`. The field IS declared `u8`, but the integer promotion to `int` makes `>>` an arithmetic shift, and MWCC emitted `srawi` against the target's `srwi`. Casting before the shift -- `(u32)fielder->maxAccLength_ConstF >> 1` bound to a `u32` local -- restores `srwi`. This is a narrower cousin of the declared-width lever: the field's declared type is right, but the EXPRESSION's promoted type is what picks the shift. Check every `>>` whose result differs by opcode.

### Fourth finding: FMA defusion by naming the two products (per call site, as always)

Target emitted `fmuls f2,f3,f3` ; `fmuls f1,f1,f1` ; `fadds f4,f2,f1`; ours fused to `fmuls` + `fmadds`. Binding both products to named `f32` locals (`dxSq = dx*dx; dzSq = dz*dz; dist = fielderSqrt(dxSq + dzSq);`) defused it. Session 4 measured the same shape as a REGRESSION on `setIntendedLocToInterceptBall`, so this is per-call-site like every other float lever in this file -- but when the target visibly does NOT fuse, naming the products is the way to stop MWCC from fusing. Combined with the `srwi` fix above: 93.89474% -> 99.68421%, and closed the last 4 bytes (376 -> exactly 380).

### Fifth finding: an external callee with NO C definition at all does NOT block; only an EMPTY STUB body blocks

Session 13 established that an external callee which is an empty `return;` stub in `src\` blocks exactly like an in-file stub (`initFielders` on `setFielderValues`). The converse also needs stating: a callee that lives in a not-yet-decompiled unit and has no `src\` definition whatsoever does NOT block, because there is no stub body for MWCC to inline away. `fieldingRelatedAnimations` is such a symbol; `fn_3_2F7D4` (94.64%) and `fn_3_258D8` (95.5%) both call it and both reach exact byte-size parity. When triaging the queue, the question is "is there an empty stub body?", not "is there a definition?".

### Sixth finding: giving a stub callee a real body can LOWER a partially-matched caller's score, and that is correct

Implementing `clamberJumpOffWall` moved `updateFielderPositionAndVelocityForSpecialActions` 92.54569% -> 92.21932%. That hub calls it; restoring a real callee body restores a call site the hub had previously optimised away, changing the hub's codegen. A naive "revert on any regression" gate reverted a +95-point gain over a -0.33 dip; that revert was overridden deliberately. Per session 3's finding (b), a hub's own score is not a meaningful metric while its other callees are stubs (this one still has six). Judge the trade by total, and record the accepted dip.

### THE session-16 finding worth carrying to other files: exit-block SHARING is a separate lever from exit-block COUNT

Sessions 12 and 13 established that each textual `return <const>;` costs its own exit block, that `(our size - target size) / 8` counts the excess, and that groupings hitting the right size can still score very differently. `fn_3_3CB8C` adds the third and final piece: **two builds can have the identical number of exit blocks, at identical sizes, and still differ in WHICH block each branch is threaded to.**

It sat at 99.863014% with exact 292/292 bytes and exactly two mismatch rows, both `blt` instructions differing only in branch target. Both objects contained the same six `li r3,0x0; blr` blocks. The target threads `landingSpotZoneAwayFromHome < 1` and the then-arm's `fielderIndex < 6` onto the SAME exit block the `else if` arm falls into, while keeping the `(landingSpotAngle < 0x380 && fielderIndex == 6)` clause on its own block. Our `||`-chain put all three of the then-arm's conditions on the near block.

The fix is to make the two conditions literally share the else-arm's `return` statement, with `goto`:
```c
    if (g_Ball.AtBat_ContactResult == 0) {
        if (g_Ball.landingSpotZoneAwayFromHome < 1 || fielderIndex < 6) {
            goto fail;
        }
        if (g_Ball.landingSpotAngle < 0x380 && fielderIndex == 6) {
            return 0;
        }
        if (g_Ball.landingSpotAngle > 0x480 && fielderIndex == 8) {
            return 0;
        }
    } else if (fielderIndex < 6 || fielderIndex != g_FieldingLogic.secondaryFielderStored) {
    fail:
        return 0;
    }
```
-> **100%**, first attempt. Note the label sits INSIDE the `else if` body and is jumped to from the `if` body; that is valid C, MWCC accepts it without diagnostic, and it is the only construct that expresses "these conditions share that arm's return" at source level. Generalisation: when two exit blocks are byte-identical and the only diff rows are branch targets, do not go looking for a different condition grouping — the count is already right. Ask which textual `return` the target's branch belongs to, and use `goto` to make the source say exactly that.

### Second finding: `fn_3_417D4` — the FMA lever again, diagnosable from the byte delta

`fn_3_417D4` was 420 B against a 424 B target, exactly one instruction short, and the target emitted `fmuls f2,f3,f3` ; `fmuls f1,f1,f1` ; `fadds f4,f2,f1` where ours emitted `fmuls` + `fmadds`. That fused instruction WAS the 4-byte shortfall. Binding both products to named locals (`dxSq`/`dzSq`) defused it: **91.471695% -> 95.28302%**, exact size, and it also corrected the load ordering — our build had been emitting the z-component subtraction before the x-component because the fusion made the last-computed operand the addend. Per-call-site as always.

### Third finding (CORRECTS session 10): `fielderSqrt` on `updateOutfielderPositionBasedOnBallState` is now POSITIVE

Session 10 measured substituting the TU-local `fielderSqrt` for `dolsqrtf2` in this function as a regression (99.71 -> 98.92) and recorded it as such. That measurement is STALE and should not be relied on: it predates session 11's rewrite of `fielderSqrt` to bind its two Newton-iteration constants to named `f64` locals, which changed the helper's FPR allocation at every call site. Re-measured this session under the corrected helper: **99.71223% -> 99.78417%**, clearing both anonymous-`@NNNN` constant-pool rows with zero regressions.

General lesson: when a shared helper is rewritten, every previously-measured negative that involved that helper is invalidated. Sweep them again rather than trusting the log.

### Negative result, PERMANENTLY CLOSED: dropping `const` from `lbl_3_rodata_B20`

The theory was attractive and is now dead. Across `fn_3_308B8`, `fn_3_417D4`, `fn_3_3ABF0`, `adjustPlayerPosOutsideFoulLine` and `toyfieldRelated`, the residual has the same shape: our build hoists the `lbl_3_rodata_B20` load to the top of the function and keeps it cached in a register, where the target re-materialises it later, at a point where an earlier value's register has died. That is textbook alias-analysis behaviour, and session 10's `const`-on-extern lever is the obvious suspect, so `extern const f32 lbl_3_rodata_B20;` was changed to `extern f32 lbl_3_rodata_B20;` and measured file-wide.

Session 11's finding — bind an inlined helper's file-scope-extern constants to named locals to control FPR allocation — does NOT generalise to a plain `f32` constant in an ordinary function. On `fn_3_308B8`, `f32 zero = lbl_3_rodata_B20;` used at all four sites compiled BYTE-IDENTICALLY to the bare extern, with the local declared first AND with it declared last. ### The auto-coords family: `fn_3_308B8` / `setFielderAutoCoords` / `fn_3_42850`

These three are the SAME function body written three times (set a fielder's `IntendedLocation` from an x/z pair; if the delta is exactly zero, zero `currentVelocity`/`distanceFromAutoLocation`, otherwise set `desiredMovementDirection2` from `ATAN2F` and `distanceFromAutoLocation` from `fielderSqrt`). `fn_3_308B8` and `setFielderAutoCoords` take x/z as parameters; `fn_3_42850` reads them from `g_Ball.AtBat_Contact_BallPos`.

**A real logic-shape difference was found and fixed in `setFielderAutoCoords`.** Its `goingToAutoLocationInd = 1;` was inside the `else` arm. The target proves it is unconditional: both arms converge on a shared join block doing `li r0,0x1` / `stb r0, 0x1d9(r31)` before the epilogue, and the then-arm's `b` jumps to that join, not to the epilogue. `fn_3_42850` already had the correct unconditional shape. Moving the store out of the `else` cleared the one branch row: 99.51923% -> 99.56731%.

**Do NOT make the same change to `fn_3_308B8`.** Its target genuinely keeps that store inside the else arm — its `stb r0, 0x1d9(r31)` sits before the shared epilogue label and is reached only from the else path. The three functions are not identical in the target, and this is the one place they differ. Verified directly from the disassembly.

Residual on all three, identical in shape: a 3-way FPR rotation. Target allocates {constant -> f0, `pos.x` -> f4, `pos.z` -> f3}; ours allocates {constant -> f4, `pos.x` -> f3, `pos.z` -> f0}. Same opcodes, same offsets, same order, same count, exact byte size. Both sides emit the constant's load at the same instruction index — only the colour differs, so this is an allocation-REQUEST-order difference, not a scheduling one: the target requests registers for `pos.x` and `pos.z` before the constant, ours requests the constant first. `fn_3_42850` carries the same rotation plus a GPR permutation (target: `g_Ball` base -> r7, `mulli` result -> r6; ours: `g_Ball` base -> r5, `mulli` -> r7).

Hypotheses tried and closed:
  [1] `f32 zero = lbl_3_rodata_B20;` local, declared first -> byte-identical (reverted)
  [2] same, declared last -> byte-identical (reverted)
  [3] drop `const` from the extern, file-wide -> no effect on any of the three (reverted; see the permanently-closed negative above)

STATUS: all three `pending`, NOT exhausted, but the lever is unidentified. An asm census this session found the target puts this constant in f0 in well over 100 sites across the unit and in f1/f2/f31 in a real minority (`wallJumpInitialization`, `jumpSetPosAndVelo`, `setFielderVelocity`, `updateFielderPosition_checkFielderCollision`, `calculateMinDiveDistAndEndingCoords` and others), so f0 is not a hard rule — but within this exact code shape it is completely consistent. Whoever reopens this needs a new idea about what makes MWCC request a global-constant load's register before versus after the surrounding value temporaries. Do not retry [1], [2] or [3].

### Session 16 addendum: the `fielderSqrt` re-sweep, and a cross-function coupling warning

Acting on this session's own finding that session 11's rewrite of `fielderSqrt` invalidated every earlier measurement involving it, all remaining `dolsqrtf2` call sites in the file were re-tested one function at a time. Five functions / seven call sites were enumerated and every one was measured.

| function | sites | before | after | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| updateFielderPosition_checkFielderCollision | 2 | 93.18227% | **93.23153%** | KEPT |
| setIntendedLocToInterceptBall | 2 | 81.82478% | **82.48718%** | KEPT |
| updateFielderPositionAndVelocityForSpecialActions | 1 | 92.21932% | 92.24543% | REVERTED — see below |
| fielderAIAssignmentRelated | 1 | 91.196075% | 91.039215% | REVERTED |
| findClosestFieldersToLooseBallAndAssignToGoGetIt | 1 | 88.93031% | 88.72125% | REVERTED |

So the lever remains genuinely per-call-site — two of five wanted the TU-local clone and three wanted the shared header inline. Session 10's blanket "net negative file-wide" conclusion is superseded: it is neither a file-wide win nor a file-wide loss, and each site must be measured. The two remaining `dolsqrtf2` sites that were tested and rejected should NOT be retried unless the helper is modified again.

**IMPORTANT cross-function coupling, newly observed and worth carrying to other files.** Switching the single call site inside `updateFielderPositionAndVelocityForSpecialActions` IMPROVED that function (92.21932% -> 92.24543%) but simultaneously regressed three unrelated functions elsewhere in the unit:
```
fielderAIAssignmentRelated:                        91.196075 -> 91.07843
setIntendedLocToInterceptBall:                     81.82478  -> 81.568375
findClosestFieldersToLooseBallAndAssignToGoGetIt:  88.93031  -> 88.82578
```
It was reverted on that basis, correctly — the change was a net loss even though its own target improved. The mechanism is that swapping which sqrt helper a call site uses changes the TU's anonymous constant-pool composition, and other functions that reference pooled entries shift with it. Consequence: **a constant-pool-affecting change can never be judged on its target function alone.** Verify all functions in the unit after any edit that adds, removes or renames a pooled constant — a watchlist is not sufficient here.

Also measured and REVERTED this session: reversing the operand order of `fRunningTimeToDestinationPlus7`'s early-return equality guard to `fielder->pos.x == x && fielder->pos.z == z` -> 99.47369% (regression from 99.68421%; it added two new `fcmpu` mismatch rows without clearing any of the four `fsubs`/`fmuls` rows it was aimed at). Do not retry.

### Durable finding: dead loop-entry guard on fully-unrolled fixed-trip-count loops (recurring)

Two functions in this file this session (fielderResetAndStoreValuesEachFrame, earlier in
Session 17, and fn_3_3E468, this entry) both have a target-side fully-unrolled
9-iteration loop block preceded by a genuine, non-optimized-away 3-instruction
(12 byte) loop-entry guard that only exists to check a trip count the compiler otherwise
proves is always non-zero. Every C-level restructuring tried across both functions this
session (an explicit guard before a do-while, a plain for loop, a while loop, a
less-or-equal-8 versus a strict-less-than-9 bound) either fails to reproduce the guard at
all (MWCC folds it away, matching neither function) or actively regresses other rows when
forcing an explicit runtime check. By contrast, processFielderAutoCatch elsewhere in this
same file uses the exact same 9-iteration unrolled loop shape and compiles with no guard
at all in the target, confirming this is not simply a property of the loop shape itself --
something about these two specific functions (possibly unrelated surrounding code,
register pressure, or an MWCC scheduling heuristic tied to what follows the loop) causes
the guard to survive in the real target binary in a way that is not reproducible from the
loop's C source in isolation. Treat this as an open, cross-function, likely
non-source-level issue (a compiler flag or version artifact) rather than something to keep
re-attempting per function; it costs a fixed, comprehensible 12 byte, 3-row gap on both
known-affected functions and should not block moving on to other targets.

### Session 17 correction: the g_Ball 0x354 "unresolved padding blob" was a red herring

`g_Ball + n*16 + 0x354` / `+ 0x35c` (the input-coordinate source used by fn_3_42A00) is
fully and correctly named already: `g_Ball.physicsSubstruct.futureCoordsAndDist[n].pos.x`
/ `.pos.z`. The arithmetic: `InMemBallType.physicsSubstruct` sits at offset 0x180;
`pastAndFutureCoordsWallJumpRelated.futureCoordsAndDist[360]` sits at relative offset
0x1D4 inside that substruct, so element 0 of the array lands at 0x180 + 0x1D4 = 0x354;
`CoordAndDist` (`{ VecXYZ pos; f32 dist; }`) is 16 bytes, exactly matching the `n*16`
stride seen in the disassembly (`slwi r0, r0, 4`); `.pos.x` sits at relative +0 (absolute
0x354) and `.pos.z` at relative +8 (absolute 0x35C). This is corroborated by ten other
call sites already in `src\` that reference this exact field by name, including
`src\game\fielding\fielder.c:1878` (`setIntendedLocToInterceptBall`), which indexes
it by the SAME expression `fielder->framesRemainingToGetToLandingSpot` that fn_3_42A00
uses. A previous analyst had flagged a `_34E[40]` padding blob near this offset as
evidence the region was unresolved -- that blob belongs to a DIFFERENT struct,
`_MiniGameStruct`, not to `InMemBallType`, and does not overlap `physicsSubstruct` at all.
General lesson: when an offset appears to land inside a flagged padding/unresolved blob,
confirm the blob actually belongs to the struct you are indexing into before concluding
the offset is unresolved -- it may belong to an unrelated sibling struct that merely
shares a numeric range in notes.

### `fn_3_468DC` exit-block lesson (worked example, recorded for reuse)

Reaching 100.000000% on `fn_3_468DC` (see the hypothesis log above) required three
distinct corrections to the task's own draft body, all in the same lever family
(exit-block count and threading), none of them float/register related:
1. The two early success paths (`fielderWBallIndex >= 0` and
   `fielderAboutToGetBall_hasBall >= 0`) had to `goto` a SHARED trailing `return 1;`
   rather than each spelling out its own textual `return 1;` -- the target genuinely
   compiles both paths into jumps to one shared `li r3,0x1; blr` block, not three
   separate ones.
2. Each pair of `== -1` checks had to be written as ONE combined condition,
   `if (A == -1 || B == -1) return 0;`, rather than two sequential `if (A == -1)
   return 0; if (B == -1) return 0;` statements -- MWCC only shares/CSEs the exit into
   one `li r3,0x0; blr` block when the pair is a single combined condition; two
   sequential ifs each get their own duplicate exit block, costing 16 bytes total (8
   bytes each) versus the target.
3. Each `>=`-based two-fielder comparison arm had to be INVERTED to the `<` sense
   (`if (A < B) { use A } else { use B }` instead of `if (A >= B) { use B } else
   { use A }`) to match the target's actual then/else block layout (its skip-branch
   targets the second-listed fielder's block, meaning the arm order and comparison
   sense both needed inverting together, not independently).
This is a clean, reusable worked example of the exit-block-count-plus-threading lever
described generally elsewhere in this file's hypothesis logs -- worth pointing at
directly rather than re-deriving from scratch on the next multi-return-path candidate.

### THE session's main finding: non-volatile FPR colour follows DECLARATION order (PROMOTION CANDIDATE for docs/matching_notes.md)

Write this up as the headline durable finding. Content: in this TU, MWCC assigns
non-volatile floating-point registers f31-downward in **order of local-variable
DECLARATION** — the first-declared long-lived `f32` local gets `f31`, the next gets `f30`.
**Assignment/statement order is NOT the lever** (already a closed negative from session
17). Swapping only the DECLARATION order of the two delta locals so the z-delta is
declared before the x-delta (a one-token change, `f32 dx; f32 dz;` -> `f32 dz; f32 dx;`)
improved three functions simultaneously with zero regressions: `fn_3_3C270`
99.3609->99.73684, `fn_3_42A00` 99.18104->99.61207, `fn_3_4597C` 98.778625->99.16031. This
is the first working lever ever found against the long-standing FP register-colour
rotation in this file. Note it was INERT on
`fielderMovement_adjustPlaceToStandForBallBouncingOffWall` (byte-identical, reverted) — so
it applies to the shared-idiom cluster, not universally. Also note explicitly that session
15b had found declaration order *inert* for GPR spill-reload colouring; that is a genuinely
different mechanism and does not contradict this.

### Closed negative: volatile FPR colour (f0/f1/f2) does NOT respond to declaration order — do not retry

Three structurally distinct hypotheses, all on `fn_3_3C270`, all reverted byte-identical:
- [1] bind the zero constant to a named `f32 zero = lbl_3_rodata_B20;` declared FIRST among
  all float locals, used at all four sites (both `fcmpu` compares and both `stfs` stores)
  -> 99.73684% -> **92.25564%** (sharp regression; introducing the named local recoloured
  `fielder->pos` accesses too). Reverted.
- [2] cache `pos.x`/`pos.z` into named `f32` locals declared AFTER both deltas, assigned
  immediately before the subtractions -> **no change at all**. Reverted.
- [3] swap the order of the two `= lbl_3_rodata_B20` store statements inside the if-block to
  alter the constant's live range -> 99.646614% (regression). Reverted.

VERDICT: the declaration-order lever governs non-volatile FPRs only. The remaining
`f0`<->`f2` swap (target: `f0`=the 0.0f constant, `f2`=`pos.x`; ours: reversed) on
`fn_3_3C270`/`fn_3_42A00`/`fn_3_4597C`/`fn_3_308B8`/`setFielderAutoCoords`/`fn_3_42850` is
NOT reachable from declaration order, assignment order, or live-range shaping. A genuinely
different mechanism class is needed (compiler flags scoped to the file, or accept as a
closed residual). Do not retry these three shapes.

### New lever: guard polarity extends to FLOAT comparisons (worked example, closed a function to 100%)

The existing guard-polarity lever was recorded only for a `cror` on the TARGET side. The
mirror case is equally actionable and is new: **a `cror eq,lt,eq` / `cror eq,gt,eq` on OUR
side where the target has a plain `bgt`/`blt` means our source wrote `<=`/`>=` where the
target negates a STRICT comparison.** On floats, `<=` forces MWCC to OR the `lt` and `eq`
condition bits (hence the `cror`), while the target's `bgt`/`blt` test `>` and `<` directly
and branch away. Rewriting
`if (collided == 2 && scratch.x <= lbl_3_rodata_B18 && scratch.x >= lbl_3_rodata_B1C)`
as
`if (collided == 2 && !(scratch.x > lbl_3_rodata_B18) && !(scratch.x < lbl_3_rodata_B1C))`
took `knockOut_setPosAndVelo` from 98.125% (456 B, 8 B over) to **100% (448 B exact)** on
the first try. Note a plain De Morgan rewrite (`!=`/`||`, arms swapped) WITHOUT the
strict-comparison change had already been tried and regressed to 88.86% — the
strict-comparison negation is the operative part, not the arm swap.

### New lever refinement: cached pointer local vs direct indexing is a PER-ACCESS-SITE judgement

The file's standing guidance prefers `InMemFielder* fielder = &g_Fielders[i];`. A
counterexample was found: on `fielderUpdateChasingRunnerValues`, REMOVING the cached
`InMemRunnerType* targetRunner` local and using direct `g_Runners[someRunnerNum]` indexing
at each of four field accesses took it 99.60145% -> **100%**. Root cause: the pointer local
created a live range that made MWCC colour the persistent `&g_FieldingLogic` pointer and
the ephemeral index-scaling temp into r4/r5 swapped relative to the target. Judge per
access site from the disassembly (does the target re-derive the base, or reuse it?) rather
than defaulting to the pointer form.

### The `setPosAndVelo` family skeleton — now proven at 100%, reuse verbatim

`knockOut_setPosAndVelo` (448 B, 100%) is the template for four still-stub siblings:
`runningCatch_updatePositionAndVelocity` (472 B), `fielderOnFirePosAndVelo` (508 B),
`jumpSetPosAndVelo` (608 B), `wallSplat_setPosAndVelo` (632 B). Record the shared shape:
1. Saturating-increment a per-state `s16` count-up field (cap `0x7fff`), then
   unconditionally decrement the paired countdown, then dispatch on the state byte. (For
   knockOut these are `knockOutCountUp`@0x1BE / `knockOutCountDown`@0x1C0 /
   `knockoutStatus`@0x210 — each sibling owns its own field triple, NOT a universal
   0x1B4/0x207 pairing.)
2. Active state: scale a stored magnitude by a `fielderActionConstants[]` entry,
   `getComponentsFromSAng(angle, &fielder->xMovementDir, &fielder->zMovementDir)`, then
   `velocityX = xMovementDir * currentVelocity; velocityZ = zMovementDir * currentVelocity;`.
3. The shared collision block — **confirmed byte-identical across siblings, reuse this
   exact arm order and polarity, which is what reached 100%**: call
   `updateFielderPosition_checkFielderCollision(fielderIndex, &scratch)`, then test
   `collided != 0` FIRST (the `collided == 0` "advance position" block goes LAST, falling
   into the shared tail), with the inner guard written `collided == 2 && !(scratch.x >
   lbl_3_rodata_B18) && !(scratch.x < lbl_3_rodata_B1C)` (the +/-55 bounds), else zero
   `currentVelocity`/`velocityX`/`velocityZ`; then the tail `IntendedLocation.x = pos.x;
   IntendedLocation.z = pos.z;`. Keep it duplicated per function — the target inlines it
   identically rather than sharing a helper.
4. Countdown-expired sub-branch: must be written as an explicit EARLY `return;` placed
   BEFORE the main body, not as an `else` arm — the target branches straight to the
   epilogue, skipping the `IntendedLocation` tail. Writing it as an `else` arm cost 16
   percentage points (65.75% vs 81.91%).

### MAJOR FINDING: the real dominant idiom in this file is the inlined `fielderSqrt` + float-classification helper

A systematic clustering pass was run over the target disassembly of all 223 functions
(normalise each function's instruction stream — registers/immediates/branch targets erased,
`bl` symbol names KEPT — then pairwise `difflib.SequenceMatcher` over all 24,753 function
pairs to find maximal common blocks, then extend each validated group STRICTLY, stopping the
instant any member of the starting group disagrees).

METHOD WARNING worth reusing: a naive "hash fixed-size windows, keep those shared by >=3
functions, greedily extend by per-position majority vote" approach produced 103 plausible-looking
clusters and FAILED the sanity check — it did not rediscover the known `fn_3_3C270`/`fn_3_4597C`/
`fn_3_42A00` triple at all. Root cause: once a validated group hits a divergence point, the
greedy extender silently switches allegiance to whatever different subset shares the next token
by coincidence. Always sanity-check a clustering method against idioms you already know exist.

The dominant result: the "safe sqrt of a squared magnitude + float classification" block —
`frsqrte` -> 3x (`fmul`,`fmul`,`fnmsub`) -> `frsp`, then a compare against `lbl_3_rodata_B40`
that forces `__float_nan` on overflow, then a manual float-bit classification chain
(`rlwinm`/`cmpw`/`clrlwi.` producing a 0-5 status code) — is shared by **up to 107 of the 223
functions**, roughly 90 of which are still stubs. This is the existing `static inline fielderSqrt`
helper being inlined identically everywhere. The session-17 "308-byte 3-function idiom" is just
this block plus a `bl atan2` delta-vector preamble; that variant alone is shared by **24**
functions, not 3. Solved members available to copy the surrounding call-site shape from include
`knockOut_setPosAndVelo` (100%), `fn_3_2D308` (100%), `fn_3_3C270` (99.74%), `fn_3_42A00`
(99.61%), `fRunningTimeToDestinationPlus7` (99.68%), `setFielderAutoCoords`/`fn_3_308B8` (99.57%).

### NEW LEVERS PROVEN THIS SESSION (promotion candidates for docs/matching_notes.md)

**1. Named temporaries defeat MWCC's `fmadds` fusion — worth up to 28 bytes and 2.7 points.**
MWCC fuses `a*b + c` into a single `fmadds`. Where the TARGET keeps a separate `fmuls` (or two)
followed by `fadds`, the original source gave each product its own named local. Recipe:
`f32 sqx = dx * dx; f32 sqz = dz * dz; ... fielderSqrt(sqx + sqz);` instead of
`fielderSqrt(dx * dx + dz * dz)`. This took `fn_3_46688` 97.28859% -> **100%**. Same lever took
`wallSplat_setPosAndVelo` from a 604-byte body to the target's exact 632 bytes by splitting
`wallActionCurrentHeight += dy * factor;` into a `heightDelta` temp plus a separate add.
IMPORTANT — it is NOT universal and must be measured per site: it REGRESSED
`calculateMinDiveDistAndEndingCoords` (97.84375 -> 97.75) and `determineBestFrameForFielder`
(83.98 -> 78.77). Apply it only where the target visibly does not fuse.

**2. Single shared exit: an if/else-if chain, not multiple early returns.** When ours emits
`li r3,N` at several early-return sites but the target emits it exactly ONCE at a shared tail,
the source used an if / else-if / ... / else chain (or loop `break`s) where every arm falls
through to ONE trailing `return`. On `fn_3_46688` this was worth 93.093956% -> 96.58389%
(3.5 points) with no other change. This is the counting/grouping exit-block lever generalised
to the return VALUE, not just the exit block.

**3. Re-deriving a struct base pointer a second time, across a call boundary.** The existing
"cached pointer local vs direct indexing is a per-access-site judgement" finding extends
further: sometimes the right answer is to assign the SAME pointer local a SECOND time
(`fielder = &g_Fielders[0];` again) immediately before a block that is live across a call,
rather than either keeping one long-lived pointer or indexing directly. The target reloads the
base into a second register after the call; re-assigning reproduces that. Took `fn_3_4CFB0`
95.89% -> 98.71%. Judge from whether the target reloads the base after a `bl`.

**4. Guard polarity — now confirmed in BOTH directions, and it is a routine first move.**
- `cror eq,lt,eq` on OUR side + plain `bgt`/`blt` on target => source needs NEGATED STRICT
  `!(x > A)`. (Took `fn_3_52084` 98.01 -> 98.41 via `!(perpDistSq < B20)` for `>=`.)
- `cror` on the TARGET side + a plain branch on ours => source wants the plain NON-STRICT
  `x <= A`. This is the mirror case and it is equally real: it took `fn_3_46688`
  96.58389 -> 97.28859.
- A compound `A && B` producing one `cror` where the target has two independent fallthrough
  branches means the source used NESTED ifs, not `&&`. Took `calculateMinDiveDistAndEndingCoords`
  97.1875 -> 97.84375 and shrank it 636 -> 632 B.

**5. Declared-width tell refinement: `clrlwi rN, r3, 25`.** On `wallJumpSOmething3` the sole
residual was the target masking a function's return value before comparing. Declaring the
receiving local as `s8` instead of the enum type took it 99.25% -> **99.57143%** AND fixed the
byte size (556 -> 560, exact). `u8` scored lower (99.53571%). The remaining single differing
instruction is target `clrlwi r0, r3, 25` (zero-extend the low SEVEN bits) vs our `extsb r0, r3`
— a 7-bit width, which suggests a `:7` bitfield or a 7-bit enum, not a plain `s8`/`u8`. Not
resolved; recorded as the exact open question for whoever picks this up.

### The `lbl_3_rodata_B50` / `@2222` relocation-name mismatch — DIAGNOSED, not solved

Our object emits an anonymous compiler-generated rodata label (`@2222`, `@2335`) where the
target references the named `lbl_3_rodata_B50`. This is the MWCC int-to-double conversion magic
constant behind the `xoris`/`lis 0x4330`/`stw`/`stw`/`lfd`/`fsubs` idiom, produced by casts like
`(f32)fielder->wallSplatStageCountDown`. Findings:
- objdiff DOES score these rows as mismatching: `diff_kind: "DIFF_ARG_MISMATCH"` with
  `arg_diff: [{}, {"diff_index":0}]`, because `relocation.target_symbol` resolves to differently
  named symbols on the two sides. The underlying `.rodata` BYTES are identical
  (`43 30 00 00 80 00 00 00`) — it is purely a symbol-identity mismatch.
- It costs `wallSplat_setPosAndVelo` 5 of its 20 differing rows and caps it below 100%
  independently of the FPR issue.
- **An anonymous `@N` label is NOT inherently a scoring obstacle.** Counter-example found:
  `main/Dolphin/mtx/quat`'s `C_QUATMtx` is scored 100% while our object names its local double
  constant `@63` against the target's `lbl_800E6A00` — different name AND different size (12 vs
  16) — and objdiff emits no `diff_kind` at all on those rows. So objdiff has a symbol-identity
  heuristic that succeeds there and fails here.
- The one structural difference between the working and failing cases: in `quat.c` the constant
  is referenced from exactly ONE site in the object, whereas `lbl_3_rodata_B50`/`@2222` is
  referenced from TWO sites within the same function. Offered as an observation, not a
  root-cause conclusion.
- `docs/matching_notes.md`'s "Naming a target's local rodata float label: declare it extern,
  never define it" is related but does NOT directly cover this: its trigger is a float literal
  the programmer wrote, whereas here the constant is compiler-generated for a cast idiom that
  the source never spells out. Whether an `extern const f64 lbl_3_rodata_B50;` can be threaded
  into that cast idiom at all is the open question. UNTESTED — worth one cheap experiment.

### The volatile-FPR (f0/f1/f2) rotation — precise size of the prize, measured

Three functions are STRICTLY pure f0/f1/f2 permutations, with zero
`DIFF_INSERT`/`DIFF_DELETE`/`DIFF_REPLACE` rows anywhere — every row index-aligns 1:1 and only
`DIFF_ARG_MISMATCH` appears. Cracking this ONE mechanism takes all three straight to 100%:
| function | % | differing rows |
|---|---|---|
| fn_3_3C270 | 99.73684% | 7 |
| fn_3_42A00 | 99.61207% | 9 |
| jumpSetPosAndVelo | 99.60526% | 10 |
`wallSplat_setPosAndVelo` (99.20886%) would go from 20 differing rows to 5 (the `@2222` rows).
`fn_3_4CFB0` (99.00662%) and `fn_3_52084` (98.4106%) are the same family with GPR swaps riding
along. Broader volatile-FPR permutations reaching outside f0-f2 (f3-f7), possibly the same
mechanism: `fielding_setStartingCoordinates` 99.87%, `fRunningTimeToDestinationPlus7` 99.68%,
`fn_3_308B8` / `setFielderAutoCoords` 99.57%, `fn_3_4597C` 99.16%, `fn_3_555AC` 98.03%,
`fielderMovement_adjustPlaceToStandForBallBouncingOffWall` 98.78%,
`adjustPlayerPosOutsideFoulLine` 95.30%. `fn_3_30A58` (97.66%) is f28-f31, a DIFFERENT
(non-volatile) mechanism.

Mechanism observation, for whoever attacks this next: in `jumpSetPosAndVelo` the ten differing
rows are ONE continuous relabeling, not three independent swaps. At the first divergence the
target loads the memory operand into f1 and the rodata constant into f0; ours does the reverse;
and that single first choice then propagates forward through every subsequent temp in the
basic-block chain. So the lever, if one exists, acts on the FIRST temp allocation of the block,
not on any individual later statement. Session 18's three closed shapes (naming the zero
constant, caching pos.x/pos.z into locals, reordering the two constant stores) all attacked
later statements — consistent with why they all failed.

**NEW LEVERS PROVEN THIS SESSION (promotion candidates for docs/matching_notes.md):**

1. **Narrow-typed locals (`s16`) fed by a narrow-returning function are usually `int` in the
   original source — worth 84 bytes in one function.** If our build emits `extsh`/`extsb` at
   every READ of a local while the target emits the extension ONCE at the assignment, the
   original declared the local as `int` and let the `s16`-returning callee's result widen at
   assignment. On `SelectBetterFielder` our five `s16` locals produced 22 redundant `extsh` = 88
   bytes of pure excess. This is the same lever family as the existing declared-width tells but
   applied in the OPPOSITE direction: the existing notes cover "target's `extsb` at use sites
   means an `s8` declared `int`"; this is "OUR `extsh` at use sites means an `int` we wrongly
   declared `s16`". Check both directions.

2. **The textually LAST `return` block falls through into the epilogue.** MWCC emits
   return-blocks in source order and lets the last one fall into the epilogue. If the target's
   final block is `return 1` and ours is `return 0`, the source put the success path last —
   reachable via `goto found;` with the body placed after the `return 0;`. On
   `clamberCheckCatch` this was worth 91.01% -> 97.30% (6.3 points) with no other change.
   Diagnostic: our `DIFF_INSERT` rows are a loop-continue + `return 0` sequence appearing at the
   tail where the target has them right after the loop guards.

3. **`SQ()` (and any macro that textually duplicates its argument) reliably SUPPRESSES
   `fmadds` fusion.** Where the target emits a fused `fmadds` and we emit `fmuls`+`fadds`, check
   for an `SQ(<computed expression>)` in the source and replace it with a named local for the
   difference. Confirmed by counter-example in the same object:
   `updateFielderPosition_checkFielderCollision` uses `SQ(...)` and BOTH sides emit the unfused
   form. This is the exact inverse of the existing "named temps defeat `fmadds` fusion" lever and
   completes it into a two-way control.

4. **MWCC lowers `L + R` (two products) so `R` becomes the standalone `fmuls` and `L` becomes
   the `fmadds` multiplier.** So when our `fmuls` holds the wrong product, the fix is to SWAP the
   two summands in the source while keeping each coefficient paired with its own operand. On
   `fn_3_54900` this took 98.62% -> 99.50% across three switch cases.
